title: Preferred Stimulation Levels in Introverts and Extraverts: Effects on Arousal and Performance
research_question: Do introverts and extraverts differ in their preferred levels of stimulation, and how do these chosen levels, as well as other assigned levels of stimulation, affect their psychophysiological arousal and performance on a paired-associates learning task?

participants.description: Male undergraduate students from introductory psychology classes at the University of Missouri-Columbia. Selected from upper and lower 25% of Eysenck Personality Inventory (EPI) E-scale scorers. Neuroticism (N) scores were controlled by assigning equal numbers of subjects scoring above and below the median to extravert and introvert groups.
participants.recruitment: Selected from a large pool of undergraduate students enrolled in introductory psychology classes who completed the EPI.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: White noise delivered in random 1-second bursts with a mean interval of 10 seconds via stereo earphones. Intensity was adjustable via a dial (0-100 units). Approximate decibel levels: Exp 1 Introvert choice ~55 dB, Extravert choice ~72 dB. Exp 2 Low ~40 dB, Mod-low ~54 dB, Mod-high ~70 dB, High ~85 dB.

measures.instrument: Dial setting (0-100 units) on tape recorder volume control switch
Standard Beckman electrodes and paste (Skin Resistance Responses, SRRs; maximum and minimum conductance levels)
Finger plethysmograph (average pulse volume, percentage of change from baseline)
Number of trials required to reach criterion (two successive errorless trials) on a 14 S-R term list

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Extravert vs. Introvert)
findings.mechanism: Extraverts are less excitable/arousable and require more intense stimulation to reach optimal arousal.
findings.quote: As predicted, extraverts chose a higher level of intensity for the bursts of noise they received than did introverts.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (chosen by self or yoked same personality type)
findings.mechanism: Subjects attain comparable optimal arousal when stimulated at their preferred level or a level chosen by their personality type.
findings.quote: The results indicate that PR in each of the assigned-same conditions did not differ from that in the appropriate choice condition.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert) at same noise intensity (Introvert-chosen or Extravert-chosen)
findings.mechanism: Introverts are more arousable than extraverts at a given level of stimulation.
findings.quote: At both levels of intensity, introverts showed higher pulse rates than extraverts.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (Introvert-chosen vs. Extravert-chosen)
findings.mechanism: Higher noise intensity leads to higher arousal.
findings.quote: An analysis of variance (ANOVA) of the data for subjects in the assigned conditions only reveals main effects for both E-I, F(1, 36) = 8.67, p < .01, and noise intensity, F(1, 36) = 9.90, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (chosen by self or yoked same personality type)
findings.mechanism: Subjects attain comparable optimal arousal when stimulated at their preferred level or a level chosen by their personality type.
findings.quote: The assigned-same condition did not differ from the choice condition. Introverts and extraverts receiving stimulation at a level chosen by members of similar personality type showed equal numbers of SRRs.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert) at same noise intensity (Introvert-chosen or Extravert-chosen)
findings.mechanism: Introverts are more arousable than extraverts at a given level of stimulation.
findings.quote: An ANOVA of the data from Figure 2 shows main effects for E-I, F(1, 36) = 7.46, p < .01, and noise intensity, F(1, 36) = 6.32, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (Introvert-chosen vs. Extravert-chosen)
findings.mechanism: Higher noise intensity leads to higher arousal.
findings.quote: An ANOVA of the data from Figure 2 shows main effects for E-I, F(1, 36) = 7.46, p < .01, and noise intensity, F(1, 36) = 6.32, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (chosen by self or yoked same personality type)
findings.mechanism: Optimal arousal levels, achieved through preferred stimulation, lead to optimal performance.
findings.quote: The mere fact of choice did not influence performance—subjects who were assigned noise equal in intensity to that chosen by their yoked counterparts in the assigned-same conditions performed as well as the latter.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert) and Noise intensity level (Introvert-chosen vs. Extravert-chosen)
findings.mechanism: Performance is best at optimal arousal. Introverts are overstimulated by extravert-preferred noise, leading to poorer performance.
findings.quote: An ANOVA showed a significant interaction between E-I and noise intensity level, F(1, 36) = 10.64, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated at Extravert-chosen noise intensity
findings.mechanism: Introverts are overstimulated by higher noise levels, leading to poorer performance (Yerkes-Dodson Law).
findings.quote: Introverts performed significantly less well than extraverts when stimulated at a level preferred by extraverts

findings.antecedent: Extraverts stimulated at Introvert-chosen noise intensity
findings.mechanism: Extraverts are understimulated by lower noise levels, but this does not significantly impair performance.
findings.quote: extraverts did not differ from introverts when stimulated at a level preferred by introverts.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Extravert vs. Introvert)
findings.mechanism: Extraverts require higher stimulation to reach their optimal arousal level.
findings.quote: The mean noise intensity setting chosen was 50.4 and that of introverts 31.1. The difference between the two means was significant, t(18) = 3.60, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Introverts' optimal noise intensity (Mod-low) vs. Introverts' lowest acceptable noise intensity (Low)
findings.mechanism: Introverts distinguish between their optimal and lowest acceptable stimulation levels.
findings.quote: The lowest acceptable intensity setting chosen by introverts was 21.1, which was significantly lower than 31.1, t(9) = 3.34, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Extraverts' optimal noise intensity (Mod-high) vs. Extraverts' highest acceptable noise intensity (High)
findings.mechanism: Extraverts distinguish between their optimal and highest acceptable stimulation levels.
findings.quote: The highest acceptable setting chosen by extraverts was 57.5, which was significantly higher than 50.4, t(9) = 4.53, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert)
findings.mechanism: Introverts have a higher baseline arousal level or are more reactive to stimulation.
findings.quote: An ANOVA of the data in Figure 3 shows significant effects for E-I, F(1, 72) = 15.50, p < .01

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High)
findings.mechanism: Higher stimulation intensity leads to increased physiological arousal.
findings.quote: the level of noise intensity, F(3, 72) = 17.98, p < .01

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert) and Noise intensity level (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High)
findings.mechanism: The relationship between stimulation and arousal is curvilinear, with introverts peaking at lower stimulation levels than extraverts.
findings.quote: the interaction between the two, F(3, 72) = 2.76, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert) at most intense (High) and least intense (Low) noise levels
findings.mechanism: At extreme stimulation levels, the arousal difference between introverts and extraverts diminishes, possibly due to transmarginal inhibition for introverts and continued increase for extraverts.
findings.quote: introverts were equal to extraverts in PR in response to both the most intense and least intense level of noise

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert) at intermediate (Mod-low, Mod-high) noise levels
findings.mechanism: Introverts are more aroused than extraverts at moderate stimulation levels, consistent with Eysenck's theory.
findings.quote: introverts showed higher PR in response to both of the intermediate levels of noise.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High)
findings.mechanism: Performance follows the Yerkes-Dodson Law, being optimal at moderate arousal levels.
findings.quote: An ANOVA shows significant effects for noise intensity, F(3, 72) = 4.68, p < .01

findings.antecedent: Personality type (Introvert vs. Extravert) and Noise intensity level (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High)
findings.mechanism: Optimal arousal levels for performance differ between introverts and extraverts, consistent with Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: the interaction of noise intensity with E-I, F(3, 72) = 8.29; p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated at their optimal noise intensity (Mod-low)
findings.mechanism: Performance is best at optimal arousal. Introverts perform best at their chosen optimal level.
findings.quote: Both introverts and extraverts required fewer trials to reach criterion when stimulated at an intensity level chosen by each of them.

findings.antecedent: Extraverts stimulated at their optimal noise intensity (Mod-high)
findings.mechanism: Performance is best at optimal arousal. Extraverts perform best at their chosen optimal level.
findings.quote: Both introverts and extraverts required fewer trials to reach criterion when stimulated at an intensity level chosen by each of them.

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated by noise at the two higher levels of intensity (Mod-high, High)
findings.mechanism: Introverts are overstimulated by higher noise levels, leading to impaired performance (Yerkes-Dodson Law).
findings.quote: Introverts showed poorer performance when stimulated by noise at the two higher levels of intensity

findings.antecedent: Extraverts stimulated by noise at the two lower levels of intensity (Low, Mod-low)
findings.mechanism: Extraverts are understimulated by lower noise levels, leading to impaired performance (Yerkes-Dodson Law).
findings.quote: Extraverts, however, showed a decrement in performance with deviations from the optimal level in both an upward and downward direction.

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated at suboptimal noise levels
findings.mechanism: Introverts can function better at very low stimulation levels than extraverts can at very high levels.
findings.quote: but no significant decrement when stimulated at a level below their optimal level.

mechanisms: Eysenck's theory of extraversion-introversion: Introverts are more arousable/excitable than extraverts, leading to different optimal arousal levels and preferred stimulation intensities.
Yerkes-Dodson Law: Performance on a task is best at an optimal level of arousal, with performance decreasing at both very low and very high arousal levels.

Cue utilization theory (Easterbrook): Increased arousal narrows the range of cues utilized in problem-solving, potentially enhancing attention to central cues at moderate arousal but eliminating necessary cues at very high arousal.
implementation_implications: Environmental design should consider individual differences in preferred stimulation levels, especially for tasks requiring optimal cognitive performance.
Providing choice over stimulation levels may help individuals achieve their optimal arousal for better performance.

tables.description: Mean Trials to Criterion (Experiment 1) across personality types and noise treatments (Choice, Assigned introvert choice, Assigned extravert choice).
Mean Trials to Criterion (Experiment 2) across personality types and noise conditions (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High).

limitations: The study did not examine what would have resulted had introverts been stimulated at a suboptimal level or extraverts at a superoptimal one in Experiment 1, limiting conclusions about deviations from optimal stimulation.
The operational definition of stimulus intensity (0-100 dial units) was converted to decibels post-hoc, making these figures approximations.
Conductance data in Experiment 2 were collected for only slightly more than half the subjects due to apparatus malfunction.
The study focused on E-I as the critical variable, but other research suggests impulsivity might be a more critical component linking E-I to arousability.
